LESSON 01: INTRODUCTION TO INTERNATIONAL ECONOMICS
Topic 001: What is International Economics?
International economics deals with the issues related to economic interactions between sovereign
states. International trade is a crucial concept of international economics, and this course also
discusses international trade in detail, including trade theories and how trade is happening among
the countries. Trade restrictions can disrupt the interaction between sovereign states.
There are seven basic concepts around which international economics revolve.
   •   The gains from trade
   •   The pattern of trade
   •   Protectionism
   •   The balance of payments
   •   Exchange rate determination
   •   International policy coordination
   •   The international capital market
Topic 002: The Gains from Trade
Countries sell goods and services to each other for their mutual benefit. When countries sell goods
and services to each other, this exchange is almost always to help the people of countries by
providing a wide variety of goods and services. The movement of capital goods helps developing
and developed countries import goods from developing countries. International trade also allows
countries to specialize in producing narrower ranges of goods, giving them greater efficiencies in
large-scale production.
Trade is not just limited to exchanging tangible goods but also services. People move from one
county to another for jobs and business, thus causing trade in services.

Does trade have adverse effects on the owners of the resources? International trade can adversely
affect the owners of resources that are “specific” to industries that compete with imports, that is,
cannot find alternative employment in other industries. Examples would include specialized
machinery, such as power looms made less valuable by textile imports, and workers with
specialized skills, like fishermen who find the value of their catch reduced by imported seafood.
Topic 003: The Pattern of Trade
The pattern of international trade means “who sells what to whom” has been a significant
preoccupation of international economists. The policymakers can only suggest policies related to
trade if they the depth of the effects trade has on the economy. Trade is considered an engine of
growth, and trade policies are very significant for the countries. For the optimum policy solution,
the trade patterns, trade potential, and all trade concepts related to trade become very significant.
Some factors like climate, factor intensity, etc., are easier to explain the pattern of trade. Middle
East countries usually export oil, while Brazil exports coffee. Developed countries enriched with
capital export capital intensive commodities like automobiles and aircraft. The patterns of trade
were discussed in the 19th century by Ricardo explained trade in terms of international differences
in labor productivity. In contrast, patterns of trade were explained in the 20th century based on the
availability and use of resources like land, labor, and capital. More recently, some international
economists have proposed theories suggesting a substantial random component in the pattern of
international trade.
Topic 004: How Much Trade
Since the emergence of modern nation-states in the 16th century, governments have worried about
the effect of international competition on domestic industries. The most consistent mission of
international economics has been to analyze the effects of these so-called protectionist policies—
and usually, though not always, to criticize protectionism and show the advantages of freer
international trade.
After World War II, the advanced democracies, led by the United States, pursued a broad policy
of removing barriers to international trade. The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)
between the United States, Canada, and Mexico was most notable, approved in 1993. The most
significant step was forming the World Trade Organization, which was converting General
Agreement on Tariff and Trade (GATT) in 1994. On the contrary, governments have tried to secure
domestic industry by restricting imports and subsidizing exports (anti-trade policies). The conflicts
